title: Comparison of Oscillometric and Invasive Blood Pressure Measurement in the Prone Position: A Prospective Observational Study (ProneTrial)
summary:
In large retrospective cohort studies, it has been demonstrated that both the frequency and duration of hypotensive events are associated with the occurrence of postoperative strokes, myocardial injuries, acute kidney injuries, and deaths (Bijker et al., 2012; Walsh et al., 2013; Sessler et al., 2018; Hallquist et al., 2018). For this reason, invasive blood pressure (IBP) monitoring is established in critically ill patients to enable continuous blood pressure monitoring and timely treatment of hypotension.

Like any measurement method, IBP monitoring can also be affected by artifacts. These factors include, for example, patient repositioning, manipulations of the arms (positioning, fixation, padding), kinks in the tubing system, blood in the tubing system, thrombi in the catheter, defective pressure transducers, and so on.

According to our clinical standards, non-invasive blood pressure (NIBP) monitoring should remain in place routinely, even when IBP is available. The aim is to provide a form of “cross-check” at regular intervals against the values displayed by IBP for the reasons mentioned above.

To our knowledge, no prospective studies have been conducted to date investigating whether and to what extent intraoperative prone positioning (e.g., for spinal surgery) affects blood pressure measurements. With this study, we aim to examine how prone positioning influences discrepancies in NIBP measurements compared to the “gold standard” of blood pressure monitoring, IBP, and whether such deviations can be minimized or prevented.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
•	Patients undergoing elective surgery in the prone position
	•	Patients scheduled to receive invasive blood pressure (IBP) monitoring
Exclusion criteria:
•	Patients under 18 years of age
	•	Patients undergoing emergency (non-elective) surgery
	•	Patients not receiving or not scheduled to receive invasive blood pressure (IBP) monitoring
	•	Patients for whom non-invasive blood pressure (NIBP) measurement on the upper arm is not feasible (e.g., due to a dialysis shunt)
